summary: Describes a URN namespace that lets Public Identifiers, used in SGML and XML, be expressed in URI syntax.

eli5.summary: It gives an old kind of document label a modern name that the web understands.

questions: how to encode public identifiers as urns
subtitle: Making old-style document labels work as modern web identifiers

tldr.problem: SGML and XML documents use public identifiers (text strings) to name DTDs and external entities, but public identifiers do not fit web architecture because they are not valid URIs. New standards like XSLT and XML Schema require all external identifiers to be URIs.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3151 defines a publicid URN namespace that converts public identifiers into URNs using simple character substitution rules: spaces become plus signs, slashes become colons, and special characters are percent-encoded.
tldr.outcome: Public identifiers can now be expressed in URI syntax, allowing them to work with modern specifications and tools that expect URIs. The structured nature of Formal Public Identifiers is preserved.

today: RFC 3151 is an Informational RFC from August 2001. It formalizes the publicid URN namespace, allowing legacy public identifiers from SGML and XML to work with modern URI-based tools and standards.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
In XML documents, external entities have two kinds of identifiers: a system identifier (which is a URI) and a public identifier (which is just a text string). The public identifier is the older, more global name; the system identifier is local or system-specific.

Historically this worked fine, but many modern specifications (XSLT, XML Schema, and others) require all external identifiers to be URIs. Public identifiers do not fit this requirement because they are not valid URIs. This creates a compatibility problem for existing documents that rely on public identifiers.

This RFC introduces the publicid URN namespace, which allows public identifiers to be reliably encoded as URNs. With this encoding, public identifiers can work alongside modern URI-based tools and specifications.
sections.eli5: Old XML documents use labels for things like document types. New tools require web-style addresses. This RFC shows how to turn the old labels into web addresses that modern tools understand.

sections.title: Public Identifiers and Formal Public Identifiers
sections.content:
A public identifier is any string containing only valid public identifier characters (a set defined by the XML specification). Public identifiers must be normalized: all runs of whitespace (spaces, tabs, carriage returns, newlines) are collapsed to single spaces, and leading and trailing whitespace are removed.

A Formal Public Identifier (FPI) is a structured subset of public identifiers, defined by SGML. Most FPIs have five fields in order: an owner identifier, a public text class, a public text description, a public text language or designating sequence, and an optional version. Owner identifiers typically begin with -// or +// and fields are delimited by // (except the class and description, which are separated by a space). Example: -//OASIS//DTD DocBook XML V4.1.2//EN.

The encoding algorithm preserves the structured nature of FPIs through special handling of // and ::, allowing them to be recognized without needing special knowledge of FPI syntax.
sections.eli5: Public identifiers are labels like book barcodes: a text string. Formal Public Identifiers have a special structure with owner, type, description, and language, separated by slashes.

sections.title: Encoding Public Identifiers as URNs
sections.content:
The URN syntax is urn:publicid:{transcribed-public-identifier}. The transcription rules convert the public identifier characters as follows:

Spaces become plus signs (+). The sequence // becomes a colon (:) and :: becomes a semicolon (;), preserving FPI structure. These special rules allow FPI structure to be recognized without explicit FPI parsing.

Seven characters require percent-encoding: a literal plus becomes %2B, a colon (except in ::) becomes %3A, a slash (except in //) becomes %2F, a semicolon becomes %3B, an apostrophe becomes %27, a question mark becomes %3F, a hash becomes %23, and a percent becomes %25. These rules preserve literal occurrences of characters that have special meaning in the encoding.

After normalization is performed on the public identifier, no two adjacent plus signs can occur in the resulting URN, which simplifies parsing and matching.
sections.eli5: To convert a public identifier to a URN, replace spaces with plus signs, replace double-slashes with colons, and encode special characters like %2B for plus, %3A for colon. This is reversible.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The public identifier ISO/IEC 10179:1996//DTD DSSSL Architecture//EN becomes urn:publicid:ISO%2FIEC+10179%3A1996:DTD+DSSSL+Architecture:EN. The slash in ISO/IEC is encoded as %2F, the space before 10179 becomes +, the colon in the year is %3A, and // becomes :.

Another example: -//OASIS//DTD DocBook XML V4.1.2//EN becomes urn:publicid:-:OASIS:DTD+DocBook+XML+V4.1.2:EN. The leading minus stays as-is, the first // becomes :, spaces become +, and the second // becomes :.

A simple identifier like foo becomes urn:publicid:foo. An identifier with a literal plus like 3+3=6 becomes urn:publicid:3%2B3=6.
sections.eli5: Real examples show how spaces become plus signs, slashes become colons, and special characters get the % treatment.

sections.title: Using and Resolving publicid URNs
sections.content:
Public identifiers can be resolved using the same methods as before: catalog files (such as OASIS TR9401 catalogs), by mapping components to file paths, or by having a system that knows a fixed set of public identifiers. URNs in the publicid namespace may also be resolvable through other URI mechanisms like caches.

URNs in the namespace are lexically equivalent if and only if they are lexically identical, because whitespace normalization is required before constructing a URN. The identifier uniqueness and persistence of publicid URNs depend on the underlying public identifiers: Formal Public Identifiers with registered owner identifiers are required to be unique and persistent, while informal public identifiers may not be.
sections.eli5: Tools can look up a urn:publicid: URN the same way they used to look up the original public identifier, using catalog files or built-in knowledge.

viz.caption: Encoding rules for public identifiers to URNs

data.title: Character transformation rules
data.code:
Public ID char  ->  URN encoding

Space           ->  +
//              ->  :
::              ->  ;
Literal +       ->  %2B
Literal :       ->  %3A
Literal /       ->  %2F
Literal ;       ->  %3B
Literal '       ->  %27
Literal ?       ->  %3F
Literal #       ->  %23
Literal %       ->  %25
